FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Recognize the indications and contraindications for medial and lateral unicompartmental knee
arthroplasty.
Outline the advantages and disadvantages of unicompartmental knee arthroplasty compared
with total knee arthroplasty.
Recognize the unique modes of failure of mobile-bearing and fixed-bearing unicompartmental
knee arthroplasty.
Background
Unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) was introduced in the 1950s by Duncan McKeever
but was largely abandoned by the 1970s because of high failure rates related to implant
design flaws and inconsistent indications and surgical technique.1,2

Over the past 25 to 30 years, UKA has regained popularity with improvements in implant
design, expanded indications, improved instrumentation, and improved midterm and long-
term implant survival.
Medial UKA
Indications/Contraindications
Traditional indications for medial UKA include low-demand, elderly, patients without obesity
who have minimal fixed deformity and isolated medial compartment osteoarthritis.
Several recent studies have challenged some of these indications, including age, weight, the
presence of patellofemoral arthritis, and anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) deficiency (Video 1).
Classic indications for UKA were proposed by Kozinn and Scott3 in 1989.
Noninflammatory unicompartmental osteoarthritis or spontaneous osteonecrosis
Less than 10° of varus alignment or 5° of valgus alignment
Correctable deformity
Flexion contracture less than 5°
Arc of motion greater than 90°
Intact ACL
Weight less than 82 kg
Age older than 60 years
Minimal pain at rest
Low demand (sedentary occupation)

Video 1 Gerlinger T, mod: Partial knee arthroplasty: State of the art. Presented at the Annual
Meeting of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 12-16, 2019.

Indications/Contraindications
Based on these restrictive criteria, Stern et al4 reported that only 6% of 228 patients who
underwent total knee arthroplasty (TKA) at their institution would be appropriate
candidates for UKA. Conversely, Hamilton et al5 reported the presence of one or more
contraindications in 68% of 1,000 patients who underwent UKA at their institution, with
no substantial difference in functional outcome scores or implant survival noted at 10
years postoperatively. Recently, several of the classic criteria, including weight, age, the
presence and severity of patellofemoral osteoarthritis, and ACL integrity, have been
questioned.
Obesity was proposed as a traditional contraindication for UKA because of concerns for
aseptic loosening and early reports of high failure rates in patients with obesity.6-8
However, several recent studies, including a meta-analysis, have challenged these
concerns, reporting no difference in outcomes or revision surgery in patients with a body
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:36 AM
AAOS | Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002013
3/40

mass index higher than 30 to 32 kg/m2, particularly if modern, metal-backed tibial
implants are used.5,9-11
Age younger than 60 years was classically considered a contraindication to UKA because
of concerns for higher activity level and a higher risk for revision surgery. Individual
studies have demonstrated no difference in long-term implant survival;5,12,13 however, a
recent meta-analysis identified a higher risk of revision surgery in younger patients.9 In
this meta-analysis, patients younger than 60 years had better functional outcomes with
UKA versus TKA.9 If UKA is performed in younger patients, a minimal tibial resection is
recommended because of the higher risk for revision surgery in the future.14
The presence of degenerative changes in the patellofemoral compartment previously
was considered a contraindication to medial UKA; however, several recent studies have
demonstrated acceptable results in patients with patellofemoral disease who underwent
medial UKA.5,9 Consensus recommendations from six high-volume orthopaedic
surgeons suggest that not all patellofemoral disease is created equal. Medial UKA is not
recommended for patients with severe patellofemoral disease involving the lateral facet
and/or the lateral trochlea; however, medial UKA may be acceptable in patients with
medial degenerative changes.14
ACL insufficiency is no longer considered an absolute contraindication to medial fixed-
bearing UKA, given that no evidence of functional instability or posteromedial wear is
observed on lateral weight-bearing radiographs (Figure 1). Many surgeons consider ACL
insufficiency a contraindication to mobile-bearing UKA because of the risk of bearing
dislocation. Several recent studies have demonstrated comparable results in patients
with or without an intact ACL who underwent fixed-bearing UKA.9,15,16
Most surgeons still consider patellofemoral arthritis and ACL insufficiency relative
contraindications to medial UKA.

Techniques
Preoperative Planning
A thorough patient history and physical examination should be performed to confirm the
diagnosis of medial compartment osteoarthritis or osteonecrosis.
Preoperative imaging studies primarily include a complete series of weight-bearing
radiographs, with the potential inclusion of stress radiographs, PA flexion radiographs, and
patellar radiographs.
MRI and CT are helpful in select scenarios.
Preoperative discussion and consent should always include the potential for TKA rather than
UKA based on the intraoperative assessment of the uninvolved compartments.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:36 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002013


Preoperative Planning
A detailed patient history and physical examination should reveal progressive activity-
related medial/anteromedial knee pain that improves with rest and that may be
associated with stiffness, swelling, and/or mechanical symptoms. The presence of
anterolateral knee pain that worsens with stair climbing, prolonged sitting, or squatting
may indicate symptomatic patellofemoral arthritis. The patient should be questioned
regarding response to prior treatment. Age, height, weight, body mass index, and social
history (including occupation, activity level, and tobacco use) should be recorded.
Medical and surgical history should be noted, specifically a history of inflammatory
arthritis or prior surgery on the ipsilateral extremity. A passively correctable varus
deformity should be less than 10°. Active and passive range of motion should be
examined. The patient’s gait should be observed, with attention paid to varus thrust, if
present. Ligament stability also should be evaluated, including Lachman and pivot shift
tests.
Radiographic examination includes weight-bearing AP, PA flexion, lateral, and Merchant
(sunrise) views (Figure 2). Degenerative changes should be isolated to the medial
compartment in patients with varus deformity or the lateral compartment in patients
with valgus deformity. The importance of patellofemoral osteoarthritis is a subject of
debate. Posteromedial wear observed on lateral radiographs may indicate ACL
deficiency. Valgus stress radiographs may be obtained to confirm whether a varus
deformity is correctable and if the lateral compartment is preserved.17 A valgus stress
radiograph is obtained with the knee in 20° of flexion (Figure 3). AP and lateral
radiographs can be used for templating implant size and position; however, implant size
and position ultimately will be determined intraoperatively. MRI is useful in patients in
whom osteonecrosis is known or suspected to confirm the extent of disease and can be
used to evaluate the integrity of the lateral compartment soft-tissue structures, the ACL,
and the patellofemoral articular cartilage. This information may aid in counseling
patients on the risk of failure. CT typically is reserved for patients undergoing robotic-
assisted UKA.

was obtained with the knee in slight flexion and the x-ray beam perpendicular to the
knee joint. A valgus force was placed on the knee joint to compress the lateral
compartment soft tissue. Joint space narrowing of more than 5 mm with valgus stress is
indicative of lateral compartment degenerative changes. (Reproduced from Jennings JM,
Kleeman-Forsthuber LT, Bolognesi MP: Medial unicompartmental arthroplasty of the
knee. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2019;27[5]:166-176.)
Patient Positioning
The patient is positioned supine on the surgical table, and an examination under anesthesia is
performed before incision.

Patient Positioning
The patient is placed in the supine position on the surgical table. A sterile or nonsterile
tourniquet may be placed well proximal on the ipsilateral thigh. Multiple options are
available for securing the leg, with a dynamic leg holder an option for mobile-bearing
UKA. Range of motion, ligament stability, and confirmation of ability to passively correct
coronal deformity (if any) should be evaluated during an examination under anesthesia
before making the incision. Patient positioning should account for the potential need to
convert to TKA based on intraoperative examination.
Surgical Approaches
Medial UKA can be performed via a medial parapatellar, subvastus, or midvastus arthrotomy.
All three compartments should be inspected on completion of the arthrotomy to confirm
candidacy for UKA versus TKA.

Surgical Approaches
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:36 AM
AAOS | Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002013
8/40

Medial UKA is most often performed via a paramedial incision, extending from just
above the medial pole of the patella to the medial aspect of the tibial tubercle (Figure 4).
The medial arthrotomy can be performed via a medial parapatellar, subvastus, or
midvastus approach. The distal portions of all three approaches are the same, with the
proximal aspect of the incision varying based on the relationship to the insertion of the
vastus medialis muscle belly onto the quadriceps tendon. Planning for potential future
surgical procedures, such as revision to TKA, should be considered.
Figure 4 Intraoperative photograph of a knee shows a standard paramedial incision
(dotted line) for left medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty, extending from just
superior to the medial pole of the patella to the medial aspect of the tibial tubercle. P =
patella, PT = patellar tendon, TT = tibial tubercle. (Courtesy of Vivek M. Shah, MD, Boston,
MA.)
The first step after the arthrotomy is to intraoperatively confirm that the patient is an
appropriate candidate for UKA. The fat pad and the anterior horn of the medial
meniscus are excised to allow for adequate visualization. All three compartments should
be inspected carefully for the presence and extent of degenerative changes by
subluxating the patella in midflexion. Lateral compartment changes greater than grade I
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:36 AM
AAOS | Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002013
9/40

or grade II and grade IV patellofemoral compartment changes (especially if the lateral
facet or the lateral trochlea is involved) are relative contraindications to UKA.
Techniques
Mobile-bearing and fixed-bearing designs are available, with mobile-bearing implants being
associated with the unique risk of bearing dislocation.
Appropriate implant alignment and surgical technique are important regardless of the type of
implant used.
Robotic-assisted UKA reduces the incidence of implant alignment outliers, especially for low-
volume UKA surgeons; preoperative CT is required for planning purposes for some robotic-
assisted systems.

Techniques
Similar to the surgical steps for primary TKA, peripheral and notch osteophytes are
removed early in the procedure to enable accurate balancing. Soft-tissue releases and
bony resection should be minimal to preserve normal anatomy and kinematics and to
plan for potential revision to TKA, if necessary. The goal of surgical management with
regard to implant alignment is to correct varus deformity within 1° to 2° of neutral.
Overcorrection is avoided to prevent overloading of the lateral compartment. Multiple
implant systems are available, with the option to begin with tibial or femoral preparation
based on the implants being used.
Tibial resection is performed at 90° relative to the mechanical axis of the tibia and
typically should attempt to match the patient’s posterior slope. This resection is critical
to reproduce the native biomechanics of the knee and restore appropriate balance. The
extramedullary tibial cutting guide is secured with the use of a single pin if possible
because the use of multiple pins, particularly peripheral pins, is associated with
postoperative tibial plateau stress fractures.18 The tibial resection level typically will be
approximately 2 mm below the lowest portion of the medial tibial plateau. The vertical
tibial cut should be adjacent to the medial tibial spine to maximize coverage. Care should
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:36 AM
AAOS | Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002013
10/40

be taken to not breach the posterior cortex or plunge deep to the horizontal tibial
resection level to avoid risk of fracture propagation.
Distal femoral resection can be performed with the use of an extramedullary or
intramedullary alignment guide. For intramedullary alignment, the entry hole should be
approximately 1 cm anterior and slightly medial to the femoral origin of the posterior
cruciate ligament. For extramedullary alignment, the guide is referenced relative to the
tibial resection. The rotational alignment of the femoral component should be
perpendicular relative to the tibial resection level with the knee flexed to 90°. Similar to
TKA, internal rotation of the femoral component should be avoided to prevent
maltracking and edge loading. In addition, the femoral component should be placed in a
central to slightly lateral position on the condyle for optimal tracking. The knee should be
held in 45° of flexion as the cement cures.
Medial UKA is available in fixed-bearing and mobile-bearing designs (Figures 5 and 6).
Fixed-bearing implants can be all polyethylene or metal backed. The primary advantage
of a fixed-bearing design is the relative ease of the procedure. Disadvantages of a fixed-
bearing design include the potential for edge loading with poor component positioning.
Conversely, mobile-bearing implants are designed for maximal congruency between the
femoral and tibial components, thereby reducing point contact forces; however, mobile-
bearing implants are associated with the unique, yet rare, risk of bearing dislocation
(Video 2). Robotic-assisted UKA was developed to improve component positioning and
accuracy. The Mako (Stryker) and NAVIO (Smith & Nephew) surgical systems have been
approved by the FDA for robotic-assisted UKA in the United States. Both systems
incorporate three-dimensional mapping to plan bony resection, with the Mako system
requiring a preoperative CT scan and intraoperative registration (Figure 7), and the
NAVIO system requiring only intraoperative condylar surface mapping (Figure 8).

Postoperative Management
Many patients undergo medial UKA on an outpatient basis.

Postoperative Management
Patients can fully bear weight on the surgical extremity postoperatively. Accelerated
rehabilitation is preferred, with many UKA procedures currently performed on an

prophylaxis should be used (Figure 9).

Complications
Aseptic loosening is the most common cause of early failure, whereas progression of
osteoarthritis is the most common cause of midterm and late failure
Higher case volume is associated with lower UKA failure rates if appropriate indications are
followed.

Complications
Failure of UKA typically is related to aseptic loosening, progression of osteoarthritis,
polyethylene wear, unexplained pain, instability, bearing dislocation (in mobile-bearing
implants), tibial fracture, or infection.29 Aseptic loosening is the most common cause of
early failure (fewer than 5 years) and is more commonly observed with mobile-bearing
implants than fixed-bearing implants (Figure 10). Progression of osteoarthritis is the
most common cause of late failure (more than 5 years) and is more commonly observed
with fixed-bearing implants (Figure 11). Mobile-bearing implants are less commonly
associated with failure related to polyethylene wear;29,30 however, they are associated
with the unique complication of bearing dislocation (0.3% to 4.2%)31-33 (Figure 12).

Several factors related to poor surgical technique have been attributed to higher failure
rates. Component malpositioning and malalignment have been associated with
decreased implant survival.34-36 Increased case volume is associated with improved
results, with surgeons who perform 30 or more UKA procedures per year experiencing
the lowest revision rates.37,38
Similar to TKA, infectious workup for patients with a painful UKA implant should include
serum and synovial fluid laboratory studies. Available literature on diagnostic criteria is
limited with regard to UKA; however, the Society of Unicondylar Research and
Continuing Education recommends the following thresholds for the diagnosis of
prosthetic joint infection: erythrocyte sedimentation rate greater than 27 mm/h, C-
reactive protein level greater than14 mg/L, synovial white blood cell count greater than

Compared with TKA, UKA is associated with poorer survivorship but is associated with
several notable advantages.58,59 UKA is associated with reduced morbidity and
mortality, fewer intraoperative complications, shorter length of stay, lower hospital
readmission rates within the first year postoperatively, improved functional outcomes,
higher patient satisfaction, preserved knee kinematics, and preserved bone.19,60-64
Outcomes of revision of medial UKA to TKA generally are poorer than those of primary
TKA, especially early outcomes, and better than those of revision of primary TKA;
however, such findings are inconsistent in recent literature.65 Surgeons should be
prepared with revision components, including augments and stems in this setting.

Indications/Contraindications
Ideal candidates for lateral UKA have isolated lateral compartment degenerative changes.

Indications/Contraindications
Indications and contraindications for lateral UKA are similar to those for medial UKA.
Patients should have isolated lateral compartment disease, which typically is most
apparent on standing lateral or standing PA midflexion radiographs. (Figure 13) In
contrast to medial UKA, ACL insufficiency is an absolute contraindication to lateral UKA.

Accessory portals may be used regardless whether a medial or lateral approach is used.

Surgical Approaches/Techniques
A medial or lateral parapatellar approach may be used. A lateral approach typically
allows for a smaller incision and easier gap balancing and may allow for improved
postoperative flexion.66-68 Some surgeons may prefer a medial approach because of
perceived ease and comfort with conversion to TKA (intraoperatively or in the future) if
necessary.67 A separate small lateral incision may be required for retractor placement if
a medial parapatellar approach is used. An accessory vertical incision through the
patellar tendon (in line with the fibers) may be considered for the vertical tibial cut to
allow for ideal component positioning with slight internal rotation of the tibial
component. Femoral component size and positioning (lateral and externally rotated) are
important to avoid patellar impingement. Native tibial slope should be matched. Fixed-
bearing implants are favored for lateral UKA because of increased motion in the lateral
compartment and the risk of bearing dislocation (Videos 3 and 4).
